Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Day One names the start of any class, course, or learning practice. The brand sits on the moment of beginning, the most important day of a learning relationship. Plain, modern, and immediately legible.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern edtech has moved past the era of MOOCs and pivoted to skill-specific, professional-grade learning products. The customer is a working adult who already pays for one or two subscription education products and will switch the moment one of them stops shipping.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Maven (maven.com) holds the cohort-based learning peer position. Coursera (coursera.org) sits in the marketplace tier. MasterClass (masterclass.com) does the celebrity-led content middle. Brilliant (brilliant.org) does the design-led STEM peer. We sit closest to Maven in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: Professional learning that ships skills, not certificates.
Modern.positioningRationale: Most edtech promises transformation. We promise the customer can do something today they couldn't do last week. The brand sells the shipped skill, not the credential.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Working adult. Already pays for at least one premium learning subscription. Wants the course to deliver a specific skill they can use on Monday.

dos: Show what the learner will be able to do
Name the instructor and their credentials
Use plain English in course descriptions
donts: Promise to change your career in 30 days
Photograph models holding laptops with serious faces

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A site that shows the curriculum in the first scroll. A small cohort of students per course. A printed welcome packet for every cohort. A direct line to the instructor for the duration of the course.

Modern.brandNameRationale: Acuity is a real Latin-rooted word meaning sharpness of thought, vision, or hearing. It signals precision and clarity without being literal about education. The pairing with 'Learning' as a category suffix follows the lineage of modern edtech naming (Brilliant, Curio, Brilliant Labs) — single evocative word plus plain suffix.
Modern.manifesto: Most online learning platforms confuse breadth with depth. Ten thousand courses, infinite trees of topics, a recommendation engine that nobody asked for. We made Acuity because the actual best teaching is narrow, scheduled, and sharp. The platform offers a small catalog of courses, each taught on a calendar, by a named teacher. Students arrive at the same time and progress together.
Modern.industrySummary: Online learning has split between MOOC platforms (Coursera, edX) optimizing breadth and cohort-based course providers (Maven, On Deck) optimizing community. The opening underneath is for a platform with a small, curated catalog of scheduled live courses with named teachers.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Maven (maven.com) holds the cohort-based course platform slot. On Deck (beondeck.com) plays in the founder-focused middle. Brilliant (brilliant.org) is the well-designed self-paced reference. We sit alongside Maven with a smaller catalog and a focus on named-teacher craft.
Modern.positioningStatement: Acuity Learning is a small-catalog online learning platform offering scheduled cohort courses taught by named teachers.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on catalog discipline. Twenty courses, not ten thousand. Each runs three times a year, taught live, capped at a working cohort size.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Atheneum is the older word for a place of learning, an institution combining library and salon. The brand names itself after the older tradition of considered learning, not the modern marketplace.
Luxury.story: The Atheneum began with three principals who had spent decades inside major universities and wanted to offer a more considered alternative for adult learners. The institution accepts a limited number of fellows each year. Each cohort is small. Each program is long.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end adult learning has been dominated by university executive education programs and high-end consulting-led programs. There's a parallel market for small, principal-led institutions in the older tradition. Few fellows, long programs, lasting relationships.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Harvard Business School Executive Education (exed.hbs.edu) is the institutional peer. The Aspen Institute (aspeninstitute.org) sits in the seminar-based tier. School of Life (theschooloflife.com) holds the design-led cultural learning middle. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small institution for adults pursuing considered learning across multiple seasons.

targetAudience.primary: 40 and up. Established in a career. Has the time and means to commit to a year-long program. Values the cohort, the principals, and the relationships built across the program.

dos: Address the fellow by surname
Speak in the language of the discipline
Send paper letters between seminars

Luxury.tagline: A small academy, one cohort at a time.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: A single proper-name academy with the definite article — the naming convention of established schools (The King's School, The Latymer School, The Wren Academy of Music in real life). Wren is a quiet English surname and bird-name, evocative without being aspirational. The 'The X Academy' format places the brand in the heritage education tradition.
Luxury.story: The Wren Academy is a small online academy offering year-long programs in a focused set of subjects. Each program is taught by a single principal teacher with a small support faculty. Cohorts are capped at thirty. Admission is by application.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium online education has clustered around executive education and bootcamp models. There is a quieter market for the small academy with year-long programs, application-based admission, and faculty continuity — closer to a graduate seminar than a course.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: MIT Open Learning and HBS Online represent the institutional reference. Reforge (reforge.com) holds the modern premium-cohort slot. The London Writers Salon (londonwriterssalon.com) plays in the small-academy peer position. We belong with the small academy tradition, with year-long programs and application admission.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The Wren Academy is a small online academy offering year-long programs, application-based admission, and principal-teacher continuity.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not scale. The academy runs four programs at a time, each with thirty students. Admission is by written application. The principal teacher stays with the cohort across the year.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word, single verb. Learn is what the customer is here for. The brand sits on the action, not the institution, not the platform. Plain, useful, direct.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most edtech brands have elaborate names, philosophies, and brand worlds. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the verb itself.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most edtech brands fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some Japanese cram school traditions and certain Khan Academy-adjacent practices.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A learning platform that does one thing: teach you a skill.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who want to learn a specific skill and don't need a brand world. They want the course, the price, and a finished result.

dos: Show what you'll learn
Show the time and the price
Use plain English

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Folio is a real word meaning a sheet of paper folded once, and historically a book of large format. In a learning context, it suggests both the page (the lesson) and the binding (the curriculum). One uncommon Latin-rooted word, like Notion or Linear. Reads as quiet, considered, slightly archaic.
Minimal.manifesto: Online learning platforms have grown into video-heavy, gamified, notification-driven products. We made Folio because the actual material of learning is still the page — a sheet you can read, mark up, return to. Each lesson is a folio. The product is the folio reader. No video, no quizzes, no streaks.
Minimal.industrySummary: Self-paced learning has become video-first and gamified. There is real space for a minimal platform that returns to the page as the unit — closer to a digital textbook than a video course.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Brilliant (brilliant.org) plays in the modern self-paced slot. Maven (maven.com) holds the live-cohort middle. Sub-stack-style writers (Lenny's Newsletter and similar) play in the single-author space. We sit further out — fewer features, the page is the product.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Folio is a self-paced learning platform where each lesson is a single readable sheet — no video, no quizzes, no gamification.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the learning surface to text and annotation. The reader marks up the folio. The folio stays in the library.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Vanguard signals first-mover and leadership. Learning Group names the category. The whole name reads like a real, established corporate learning firm already on the procurement panel at Fortune 500 talent and L&D teams.
Corporate.industrySummary: Corporate learning and development is a multi-billion-dollar B2B category. Companies want partners who can deliver workforce upskilling, leadership development, and compliance training at scale with operational discipline and measurable outcomes.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Cornerstone OnDemand (cornerstoneondemand.com) holds the LMS platform peer. Skillsoft (skillsoft.com) sits in the content-led tier. Korn Ferry (kornferry.com) does the strategy-and-talent middle. We sit smaller and more focused on the contemporary mid-market enterprise.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Workforce learning and leadership development for mid-market enterprise.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Mid-market companies are too small for Skillsoft attention and too sophisticated for boutique L&D consultants. We sit between them, with operating discipline and outcome reporting.

Corporate.tagline: K-12 and higher-ed learning infrastructure, enterprise-grade.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Lectern is the literal teaching object — the stand from which lectures are delivered. As a brand name it places the company firmly in the institutional teaching tradition. Education Group signals the multi-product holding-company structure with K-12, higher-ed, and adult-learning divisions under one corporate umbrella.
Corporate.manifesto: Lectern Education Group provides learning infrastructure to K-12 districts, university systems, and adult-learning providers. The buyer is a superintendent, a provost, or a director of professional development. The contract is multi-year. The metric is implementation success, ongoing support, and renewal.
Corporate.industrySummary: Enterprise education infrastructure (LMS, SIS, student lifecycle systems) is dominated by a small number of incumbents (Blackboard, Canvas, PowerSchool). The opening is for a serious mid-tier vendor with implementation depth, contract flexibility, and the procurement-friendly posture institutional buyers demand.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: PowerSchool (powerschool.com) is the K-12 incumbent. Instructure (instructure.com) holds the higher-ed reference. Blackboard (blackboard.com) is the legacy peer. We belong in the regional mid-tier institutional vendor category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Lectern Education Group provides LMS, SIS, and learner analytics platforms to K-12 districts, higher-ed institutions, and adult-learning providers.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on implementation depth, contract flexibility, and procurement readiness. The deliverable is reliable, audit-compliant, multi-year infrastructure with attentive support.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Night School names a real institution with a specific cultural memory: working adults learning after hours, not for credit, because they want to. The brand puts the older, less-credentialed tradition of evening learning in the brand position. Loud, warm, and slightly nostalgic.
Creative.manifesto: Most edtech brands sell certificates, transformations, and career changes. We made Night School because some people want to learn things for the same reason they read books: because it's interesting. The brand is for evening classes, weekend workshops, and the kind of learning that doesn't appear on a LinkedIn profile.
Creative.industrySummary: Edtech branding has been polished, credential-led, and slightly anxious. There's room for a brand that's warm, playful, sticker-friendly, and serious about the older tradition of learning-for-its-own-sake.
Creative.competitorLandscape: School of Life (theschooloflife.com) holds the closest cultural-learning peer. MasterClass (masterclass.com) does the celebrity-led version. The Strand's classes do the bookstore-adjacent middle. We sit warmer and louder than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: Learning for adults who want it for the love of it.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Real evening classes in a real building. Printed course catalogs mailed twice a year. Stickers in every welcome packet. A small bookstore at the back of the building. A monthly newsletter written by the instructors.

Creative.tagline: A small school for unusual subjects.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Owl is the academic-tradition symbol of wisdom; inkwell is the tradition's writing object. Pairing them with an ampersand creates a name that reads as a small academy or independent school, slightly literary, slightly old-fashioned. The pairing borrows from the bookshop-and-academy naming tradition (Hatchard & Co, Lutyens & Rubinstein) without imitating any of them.
Creative.manifesto: Most online education sells employable skills. We started Owl & Inkwell because the actual best learning is often unemployable — Latin etymology, medieval astronomy, the history of paper, the lost art of letter-writing. We run small live courses on subjects that will not improve your career and may improve your life. The school exists because the subject does.
Creative.industrySummary: Online education has consolidated around career-utility courses. There is real space for an unapologetically non-utility platform — courses in the humanities, classics, history, and craft, taught by enthusiasts to small live cohorts.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Hardcore History (dancarlin.com) plays in the long-form humanities space. London Writers Salon (londonwriterssalon.com) holds the small-academy peer slot. Catapult (catapult.co) sits in the writing-school middle. We sit alongside Catapult with a broader humanities footprint and a clearer literary register.
Creative.positioningStatement: Owl & Inkwell is a small live-course school offering courses in the humanities, classics, history, and craft — taught for love, not for career.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand stakes a position against career-utility learning. Course descriptions argue for the subject on its own terms. The audience is self-selecting.
